sentences.text: Only a single specimen, the holotype PVL 4077, is known from the Cañadón Asfalto Formation of Argentina.
This fossil includes partial cervical and dorsal vertebrae, part of the sacrum, incomplete tail vertebrae, partial pelvic bones, and hind limb bones including a femur and tibia.
The ilium measures 45 centimeters in length.
The size of a fully grown Volkheimeria is unknown because the known specimen is immature.
A potentially associated tooth is broad and spoon-shaped with large denticles on the upper two-thirds of the crown.
Pleurocoels, which are air sac cavities in the vertebrae, are present in the cervical vertebrae but absent in the dorsal vertebrae.
The tibia is relatively short compared to the femur, measuring only 58% of its length.
The only known specimen was found at Cerro Cóndor Sur, about a kilometer west of the village of Cerro Cóndor in Chubut Province, Argentina.
José Bonaparte described Volkheimeria chubutensis as a new genus and species in 1979.
The genus name Volkheimeria honors the Argentine paleontologist Wolfgang Volkheimer.
A 2017 histological examination of the femur indicated rapid growth with no clear growth rings.
Phylogenetic analyses have variably recovered Volkheimeria as a eusauropod, vulcanodontid, or primitive sauropod due to its incomplete nature.
Originally identified as a possible cetiosaurid and later a brachiosaurid, Volkheimeria is now considered a eusauropod, specifically a relatively primitive one compared to Patagosaurus.
Volkheimeria is classified within the unranked family Eusauropoda.
Volkheimeria belongs to the parent group Gravisauria.
Volkheimeria is classified within the class Saurischia.
Volkheimeria lived during the Toarcian age of the Early Jurassic, 178 to 179 million years ago.
